[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p49/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · عثمان بن عفان | reports | ʿUthmān told the scribes to use Quraysh’s language if they differed; they chose tāʾ in al-tābūt over Zayd’s hāʾ reading.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p49/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | In the variant al-tābūt/al-tābūh, Zayd ibn Thābit read with hāʾ and the Qurayshīs with tāʾ, so the codex adopted tāʾ.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p49/r13] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · عثمان بن عفان | reports | ʿUthmān produced codex copies for the regions and ordered the remaining codices burned or torn; an alternate transmission says buried, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the first reading.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p49/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | After many Qurʾān reciters died at al-Yamāma, ʿUmar advised Abū Bakr to compile the Qurʾān for fear that the senior reciters’ deaths would cause it to be lost.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p49/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · زيد بن ثابت | reports | Abū Bakr and ʿUmar assigned Zayd ibn Thābit to gather the text; he completed the demanding task without arranging the sūras.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p49/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · خزيمة بن ثابت | reports | A report says the last verse of Sūrat Barāʾa was missing in the first collection and found with Khuzayma; al-Ṭabarī places the loss in the later collection, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the earlier account.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p49/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · البخاري | reports | Al-Bukhārī’s version names Abū Khuzayma al-Anṣārī as the person with whom the verse was found.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p49/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · البخاري | reports | Al-Bukhārī reports that a verse from al-Aḥzāb, Among the believers are men, was missing in the second compilation until Zayd found it with Khuzayma ibn Thābit. | mentions 33:23
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p49/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The sheets passed from Abū Bakr to ʿUmar and then Ḥafṣa; meanwhile regional Companion codices differed in line with the seven aḥruf.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p49/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · البخاري | reports | Al-Bukhārī names three Qurayshī scribes who assisted Zayd for ʿUthmān: Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p49/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الطبري | reports | Al-Ṭabarī says that only Abān ibn Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ assisted Zayd; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this report weak.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The Qurʾān is also called the Book, the Criterion, and the Reminder.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قيل | reports | Another explanation is that the Qurʾān is called the Reminder because it recounts earlier nations and prophets.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قيل | reports | A further explanation is that it is an honorific remembrance for Muḥammad, his people, and the scholars who know it.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Quraysh and neighboring tribes say sūra without hamza, while Tamīm and others pronounce it with hamza as suʾr or suʾra.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r13] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | With hamza, sūra is a remainder or piece from asʾara, to leave; al-Aʿshā’s line uses the verb for a wound left in the heart.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r14] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | Among those who omit hamza, some keep the same etymology and treat the hamza as softened.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r15] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | Other non-hamza speakers derive sūra from a section of

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r16] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The plural of a Qurʾānic sūra has a fatḥa on the wāw, while the plural for a building section has a sukūn.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Ibn ʿAṭiyya takes Qurʾān as a verbal noun from qaraʾa, to recite; Abū Zayd also records the form qurʾā.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda derives Qurʾān from gathering and composing; he reads 75:17 as God’s gathering and compiling the Qurʾān. | mentions 75:17
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda’s etymology is illustrated by ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm’s line about a she-camel that has not gathered a fetus in her womb.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | prefers | Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the recitation etymology, supported by Ḥassān ibn Thābit’s use of qurʾānan to mean recitation.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Kitāb derives from kataba, to gather; a troop is called katība because its members are assembled.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The poetic phrase write them with straps means gather them together.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Furqān is a verbal noun because the Qurʾān separates truth from falsehood and believers from unbelievers.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p56/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Dhikr names the Qurʾān because it reminds people of the afterlife, God, and matters they had neglected.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p307/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The verse first points to God’s power and establishes proof against unbelievers, then makes the imagery a parable for truth and falsehood, faith and disbelief, and doubt and certainty in religion.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p307/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مكي وغيره | reports | Makki and others attach ‘in the fire’ to an omitted word meaning ‘being’ or ‘established,’ arguing that anything heated is already in the fire.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p307/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أبو علي الفارسي | reports | Abu Ali al-Farisi attaches ‘in the fire’ to ‘you heat’: an object can be heated without being in the fire, as in 28:38, where flame strikes the clay. | mentions 28:38
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p307/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The water is rain, and wadis are depressions, trenches, or low places between mountains.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p307/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The measure may be the water allotted to each valley or the capacity of each valley according to its size.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p307/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الأشهب العقيلي | reports | Most read bi-qadariha with an open dāl; al-Ashhab al-Uqayli reads it with a silent dāl.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p307/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Zabad is the flood’s debris and the foam thrown onto its banks; a line by Hassan ibn Thabit witnesses the word.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p307/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Rābi means swollen or inflated, from the same root as rabwah, a mound.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p307/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | In ‘from what you heat,’ مما is the fronted predicate and زبد the subject; مثله qualifies زبد.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p307/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Materials heated for ornaments are gold and silver; utility materials include iron, lead, copper, and similar metals, whose foam resembles flood foam.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p307/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Useful water and refined metal represent truth; discarded flood foam and escaping smoke represent falsehood.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p308/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Jufāʾ is a verbal noun from a pot boiling until its foam spills out and disappears.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p308/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · رؤبة | reports | Ruʾba reads jufālan, from a verb meaning wind carries and scatters clouds; Abu Hatim says Bedouin readings of the Quran are not to be considered.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p308/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أبو حاتم | reports | Abu Hatim says Bedouin readings of the Quran are not to be considered.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p308/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | What benefits people is the pure water and the purified useful metals or stones.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p308/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وعاصم وغيرهم | reports | Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, Asim in Abu Bakr’s narration, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Aʿraj, Shayba, and Hasan read with second-person tāʾ, addressing people who kindle.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p308/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · حمزة والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم وغيرهم | reports | Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, Hafs from Asim, Ibn Muhaysin, Mujahid, Talha, Yahya, and Kufans read with third-person yāʾ, referring to people; jufāʾ is a verbal noun used circumstantially.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p308/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن عباس | reports | A symbolic interpretation attributed to Ibn Abbas takes the water as religious law and valleys as hearts, with the intelligent and foolish each taking their share.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p308/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | rejects | Ibn Atiyya says the symbolic reading is likely not soundly transmitted and follows esoteric interpretation; absent a reason, Arabic wording should retain its ordinary sense. If sound, it means truth settles in guided hearts while misgivings and doubts intrude as people study the Book.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God gives two illustrations of truth and falsehood: water with foam, and precious metals or other materials heated in fire with their slag.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | To strike a parable is to circulate it through lands until people use it as a familiar example.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The foam goes away as useless scattered matter.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | What benefits people is pure water and useful substances; it remains in the earth and people benefit from it.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The believer and his conviction resemble life-giving water and useful gold, silver, and other substances; the unbeliever and disbelief resemble foam, slag, and metallic dross.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God gives these examples to people concerning their religion.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda counts three parables in one: Qur'an is rainwater and hearts are riverbeds, each taking an amount according to receptivity; reflection yields a great share and general assent a smaller one.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r16] TABRISI, d. 548 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda's second parable compares passing thoughts and Satan's whispers to foam above water: doubts arise from the soul, not from truth, and disappear while truth remains.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The water sent down from heaven is rain.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · الحسن وقتادة والجبائي | reports | The streams carry water in proportion to their size: a small stream to its smallness and a large one to its largeness.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj says the streams receive the amount of water apportioned to them.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The foam floats high above the water; pure useful water represents truth and Islam, while transient foam represents falsehood.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | Another model makes Qur'an the descending water, with hearts taking their share of certainty and doubt according to capacity; water is certainty and foam is doubt.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The second example concerns gold, silver, lead, and other materials melted in fire.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Adornment means ornaments made from gold and silver; useful goods include things made from minerals, such as vessels.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#2/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The heated materials also produce foam: their slag is impurity separated from the pure substance.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#3/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The third illustration makes disbelief useless dross and faith pure, beneficial water.
[TABRISI:13:17-18#3/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · الحسن والبلخي | reports | Al-Ḥasan and al-Balkhī take the parable phrase as the end of the preceding passage, then begin a new sentence with ‘For those who respond to their Lord.’
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · أهل الكوفة إلا أبا بكر | reports | The Kufans except Abū Bakr read يوقدون with yāʾ, in the third person.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | The cited poem's use of al-qadar in its line about calamities witnesses the word's form.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Iḥtimāl means lifting something on one's back with the bearer's strength; iḥtamalahu also describes a loud voice that someone bears without anger.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Zabad is the scum of boiling, including foam on a pot or flood.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Jufāʾ is long like ghuthāʾ and originally has hamza; the verbs describe a valley producing foam and a pot shedding it.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو زيد | reports | Abū Zayd says jafaʾtu a man means I knocked him down, and ajfaʾtu the pot with its foam means I removed the foam.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ says things that collect together commonly take the pattern fiʿāl, such as debris, cotton, ghuthāʾ, and jufāʾ.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r16] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Īqād is putting firewood on a fire; related forms istawqada

[TABRISI:13:17-18/r17] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Matāʿ means something used for enjoyment or benefit.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r18] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Makth is remaining somewhere as time passes; makatha, mukitha, and tamakkatha all mean to stay.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r19] TABRISI, d. 548 · جامع العلوم البصير | reports | The phrase fī al-nār is an implied circumstantial modifier of the pronoun in ʿalayhi; the sense is that the material is in the fire while being heated for adornment.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · الباقون | reports | The remaining readers use tāʾ, addressing ‘you ignite.’
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r20] TABRISI, d. 548 · جامع العلوم البصير | reports | Ibtighāʾ ḥilya is a verbal noun functioning as a circumstantial clause for the subject of yuqīdūn, meaning they seek adornment.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r21] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو علي | reports | Abū ʿAlī's analysis is that fī al-nār is not governed directly by yuqīdūn; the gold is heated while it is in the fire.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r22] TABRISI, d. 548 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh treats zabad as the subject, mithl as its adjective, and مما توقدون as its predicate.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r23] TABRISI, d. 548 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash instead treats the phrase as raised by the adverbial expression.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r24] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Jufāʾ is accusative as a circumstantial expression, describing the state in which the foam goes away.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو علي | reports | Abū ʿAlī explains the tāʾ reading from the preceding address in ‘Have you then taken?’; it may also address all people generally.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو علي | reports | The yāʾ reading follows the earlier third-person mention of those who set up partners; it can also mean all people, as ‘what benefits people’ is general.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو علي | reports | Fī al-nār modifies yuqidūn: one can kindle upon something not itself inside a fire, as in the command to kindle clay. | mentions 28:38
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | A wādī is the low ground at the base of a great mountain where rainwater gathers; diya is derived from the accumulation of substantial wealth paid for a slain person.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Qadr is a proportionate relation without addition or reduction; wazn permits increase or decrease, and equality is qadr.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan reads bi-qadrihā with sukūn on the dāl; both vocalizations are dialect forms.
[TABRISI:13:17-18/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Qadr can be used in either vocalization, as in expressions for a span's measure; people also discuss destiny using both forms.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p171/r4] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · مقاتل | reports | The seventeenth sense of earth is the heart. Muqātil says the water in the parable is the Quran, so earth denotes hearts.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p413/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Ṭughyān is exceeding a limit; anyone exceeding his limits in disobedience is a ṭāgh.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p413/r2] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | The verb describes a flood bringing a great volume of water, a sea whose waves surge, or blood swelling and flowing.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p413/r3] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl recognizes ṭughyān and ṭughwān as variant forms, with both ṭaghaytu and ṭaghawtu as verbs.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p549/r6] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · مقاتل بن سليمان | reports | Muqātil ibn Sulaymān interprets the water in the parable of 13:17 as the Qur'an, likening it to water that gives life; the source says he alone is reported to give this sense.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p558/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Matāʿ is what a person obtains to fulfill a purpose or desire; istamtaʿa means obtaining something desired by the self.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p558/r2] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Ibn Qutayba gives matāʿ the sense of duration, as in the day extending, and also uses it for useful equipment and benefit, including a divorced woman’s mutʿa.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p558/r3] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · شيخنا | reports | The teacher defines pilgrimage tamattuʿ as performing ʿumra in the pilgrimage months, then enjoying clothing, perfume, and marital relations before ḥajj.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p558/r4] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · شيخنا | reports | The teacher defines the divorced woman’s mutʿa as what is given when no dower was fixed and the marriage was not consummated.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p558/r7] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | A third sense is metal articles made for use or enjoyment, such as iron, lead, and copper.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p321/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The water sent down from heaven is rain.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p321/r10] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The material put into the fire is melted ore or precious material.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p321/r11] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The jewelry sought from the molten material is gold and silver.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p321/r12] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The useful goods include iron, brass, copper, and lead, made into vessels and other useful things.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p321/r13] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Like floodwater, molten metal produces foam; this is a second simile.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p321/r14] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | One view maps the water and valleys onto the Qur'an and human hearts, which receive according to faith, doubt, intelligence, and ignorance; believers benefit while unbelievers do not.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p321/r15] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | A second view maps the lasting clear water to truth and the vanishing foam to falsehood, which God will abolish even if it temporarily rises above truth.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p321/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Awdiya is the plural of wādin, a low passage between two mountains where rainwater gathers and flows.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p321/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Each valley carries water according to its capacity: a small valley carries little, and a broad one carries much.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p321/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الحسن وابن جبير وأبو العالية وأيوب وابن يعمر وأبو حاتم عن يعقوب | reports | Al-Ḥasan, Ibn Jubayr, Abū al-ʿĀliya, Ayyūb, Ibn Yaʿmar, and Abū Ḥātim from Yaʿqūb read bi-qadrihā with a still dāl.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p321/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The wording expands the expression by omitting the genitive nouns: the valleys' waters flowed and the water flowed according to its measure.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p321/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The foam is high, rising above the water.
